title: De la Rosa on how Aston Martin’s risky upgrades paid off
excerpt:
Pedro de la Rosa has delved into “one of the best moments we've had so far” when Fernando Alonso shared his approval of Aston Martin's upgrade package in Hungary, with the squad's Team Representative admitting that he was “very nervous” about their unique schedule.

The beginning of the season came with plenty of challenges for the Silverstone-based outfit as they struggled with reliability issues and a lack of performance, leading them to focus their efforts on delivering a B-spec of the 2026 car in Round 11.

It seemed like a bold approach, especially at a time when their rivals were spreading upgrades over multiple race weekends, but it paid off – the heavily revised AMR26 got ahead of Cadillac and Williams in Qualifying before further progress came in the form of a new Honda power unit in the Netherlands.

On the latest episode of the official F1 podcast Beyond The Grid, De la Rosa provided some insight into just how much relied on the success of the upgrades.

‘Everything worked as planned’

De la Rosa conceded that he wasn’t certain just how much performance the changes would bring, but it didn’t take long for Alonso to give his verdict.

“I would lie if I said I was not very nervous because you are expecting, you are hoping, you've been waiting a long time, and then the car just starts,” he said. “I looked at the car and the side pods were so small, the radiators look the smallest I've ever seen in my life.

“And I thought ‘OK, the aero numbers are promising, but maybe the cooling is not enough.’ Or you start thinking about many other scenarios where I've been, because I've been in most of the most unwanted scenarios in F1. But everything worked as planned.

“Then after the installation lap, you looked around and the people were relieved because everything was working as expected. With Fernando, I know him so much that we look at the eyes. I always try to be at the front of the car when he comes in after a run. He looks at me, I look at him, and I know exactly what he's thinking.

“I don't even need to listen to the radio. And his eyes look like, ‘yes, it's working.’ Sometimes we've had upgrades in the past and I look at him and he immediately doesn't want to look at my eyes. When he tries to refuse the eye contact, I know we are in trouble. But that time he looked and he was just like, ‘yeah, it's there, it's there.’

Alonso details why he's in no hurry to make call on his future

“It was a very exciting moment. You always have to focus on things you can change, you can do, you can improve. That was, OK, not where we wanted to be, I repeat again, but it was one of the best moments we've had so far this season.”

With ongoing speculation around Alonso’s future in the sport, his reaction was the boost the team needed, although De la Rosa stated that the upgrades were never going to sway the Spaniard.

Asked whether the strategy risked losing their star driver, he replied: “I think that decision was never based [on] if we lost anyone or anything. I think that Fernando, whatever his decision will be, you have to believe in a project, you know, not if the car is quick on the next race.

“I think Fernando is so wise, he's learned so much, that it's either you believe in the project or you don't. It's not whether we managed to improve the car for the summer break as we were expecting.”

Being ‘in good hands’ with Adrian Newey

One of the factors that made Aston Martin’s initial difficulties such a shock to fans was last season’s addition of Adrian Newey, who is widely regarded as one of the most successful car designers in the sport’s history.

With years of experience at teams like Williams and Red Bull, many believed that the Briton would quickly transform Aston Martin and take them closer to the front in his latest role as Team Principal.

While it hasn’t gone that way quite yet, De la Rosa was satisfied with how easily Newey has settled into the outfit and offered a new interpretation of the traditional team boss responsibilities.

How an unraced Newey-designed McLaren compares to Aston Martin’s 2026 car

“I must say that Team Principal is a title,” he explained. “It's not a job description. Adrian has said it many times. We are fortunate in the team having Mike Krack as well, an experienced Team Principal, now chief track operations.

“But when Adrian is not at the racetrack, Mike acts like a Team Principal. I think we have a very luxurious situation where we have people working in different areas covering for when Adrian is not here. Other teams have different structures.

“It's quite ambiguous now what a Team Principal job description really is. In my time, you had a Team Principal that was taking all the decisions. But now you have a Team Principal and normally you also have a CEO on top of them. I think that we have a very good structure. As long as Adrian feels comfortable and competitive, we're in good hands.”

Taking steps towards where they want to be

Aston Martin have made it clear that scrapping for points – which they’ve achieved on two occasions in 2026 with Alonso – is far from their ultimate goal, but they’ve got some catching up to do in relation to the frontrunners.

Despite De la Rosa’s admission that F1 is “a business where you arrive always too late”, he was enthused by the progress they’d made, and determined to make even more.

“I think that we are in the upward trend,” he concluded. “I've said it in Australia this year, when we started this, we were nowhere. But all we need to do is improve and never stop improving.

“Obviously, our strategy was different. We didn't improve until the summer, but we've made a big step. We are now in a position we cannot stop. It's just a race of time. The people have done a better job than us. That's why they're winning. We just have to slowly chip away all this difference. That’s where we are.

“Everyone has to feel accountable for the results. Everyone has to feel super motivated. We have an amazing partner in Honda that we've managed to survive very difficult times together. We can’t stop and we won't stop.

“We can do it. It's just a matter of never stop the development path that we are in right now. The only teams that do win are the ones that make the right investments. I believe I'm in the right team that is definitely making the right investments.”

title: 5 storylines we're excited about ahead of the Spanish GP
excerpt:
How time flies, as we reach the end of the European season with a second visit to Spain and a brand new venue in Madrid. Off the back of Kimi Antonelli’s remarkable victory in Monza, it’s time for the drivers and teams to reset for a different challenge as we head to the Madring.

A new track!

Who doesn’t love a new circuit to see the drivers put through their paces? From the iconic venue of Monza – the track that has hosted more Formula 1 World Championship races than any other – we head to the newest circuit on the calendar and the 3.365-mile Madring.

Located at the IFEMA Exhibition Centre to the north east of the centre of Madrid, the Madring is part-street circuit, part-permanent venue and will provide a very different test compared to last week’s race. There are tight and twisting complexes, flowing sections and even the heavily banked La Monumental corner that will see fans flanking both sides of the circuit as the cars turn through more than 180 degrees.

Given the proximity of the walls in so many parts of the track, mistakes will certainly be severely punished, but the drivers will need to get up to speed quickly. And they’ll do so at a track that will put a premium on slow-speed corner performance and traction, as well as how well a car can ride bumps and kerbs.

It’s going to be a steep learning curve from the moment the teams hit the track on Friday for Free Practice 1.

Advantage Antonelli in the title race

It’s true that Kimi Antonelli was in an extremely strong position in the Drivers’ Championship even before the Italian Grand Prix, but his remarkable win on Sunday has only increased his hopes of winning his first title.

Antonelli was expected to be in damage limitation mode starting 19th, with George Russell, Lewis Hamilton and Lando Norris all hoping to take points off the championship leader. But with the Italian winning his home race on the same weekend he took a power unit penalty, Antonelli now has a 66-point advantage over Russell, that extends to 76 over Hamilton and 96 over Norris.

Why Antonelli’s Monza win feels like the defining moment of 2026

As impressive as Antonelli’s drive was at Monza, we’ve seen multiple occasions this season where reliability or circumstance has led to big swings in terms of points, and there are still 10 rounds remaining as we arrive in the Spanish capital.

For Russell, the form has been more consistent since the summer break, but he needs to find that little bit more performance to put pressure on Antonelli and take regular points off his team mate. There’s still plenty of time left in the season, but the chasing pack will want to hit back quickly.

Can McLaren return to winning ways?

Given recent form, it is perhaps Norris who is likely to offer the biggest threat over the coming races, with the McLaren most competitive on the recent higher-downforce circuits of the Hungaroring and Zandvoort. Norris won on both occasions, and could be in with a chance of doing so again in Madrid.

The layout should suit McLaren more than Monza did, and despite dampening expectations before the Italian Grand Prix, both cars were in the mix for a podium until the closing stages.

That was also thanks to a strong performance from Oscar Piastri, who has yet to win this season but outqualified Norris for the first time since Monaco, and was fighting with his team mate right up to the flag.

While Mercedes appeared to be in a league of their own for spells of the race in Monza, McLaren know Madrid is the type of venue that they should be more competitive relative to the Constructors’ Championship leaders, and will look to hit back this weekend.

Another chance for Lawson and Tsunoda

After an impressive first half of the season at Red Bull, it has been a frustrating few weeks for Isack Hadjar as he has been unable to race since the summer break due to an injured wrist.

The Frenchman missed the Dutch Grand Prix soon after sustaining the injury in training, and then Red Bull opted to not rush him back for Monza as his recovery continues. While the team say his progress has been positive, they made an even earlier call this week to continue with an unchanged line-up, rather than unnecessarily take a risk with Hadjar returning on a street circuit at this stage.

That means another opportunity for Liam Lawson alongside Max Verstappen, after a frustrating weekend in Monza. Lawson took a power unit penalty so always faced a tough afternoon trying to climb through the field, but picked up damage and needed an extra pit stop that prevented him from scoring points.

Lawson did score at Zandvoort, however, and will look to repeat that result in Madrid, while Yuki Tsunoda has also been in the points since returning to VCARB. The Red Bull reserve was just one place outside the top 10 in Zandvoort, and then went one better with 10th place at Monza to secure double points for the team.

The F3 championship showdown

The European season might be coming to an end for Formula 1 this weekend, but it’s the entire 2026 championship that is concluding in Formula 3. And what a final round it promises to be.

The Madring was always scheduled to host the finale, but the postponement of the Bahrain Grand Prix earlier this year has led to a bumper weekend as an extra Qualifying session and Feature Race will take place in Spain.

The Qualifying sessions run back-to-back on Friday, with a Sprint Race on Saturday morning and then the first Feature in the evening after F1 Qualifying. Then Sunday morning will see the final round that could well prove to be a title decider.

GALLERY: F3 drivers test the 'incredible' Madring circuit

Audi-backed junior Freddie Slater arrives with a 15-point advantage over American Ugo Ugochukwu, with the pair having been locked in a close championship battle all year.

Slater looked set to open up a big lead in Monza as he started the Feature Race from pole position and Ugochukwu languished at the back following a grid penalty and early contact, but a dramatic turn of events saw Slater retire and Ugochukwu recover to finish eighth.

There is a maximum of 67 points available over the weekend - 25 for a Feature Race win, 10 for a Sprint, plus a fastest lap point in every race and two points for pole position for each Feature Race - plus Ernesto Rivera and Theophile Nael are both mathematically still in contention but both need a hugely improbable combination of results.

That means it’s likely to be a fight between rookie Slater and second-year Ugochukwu to follow in the footsteps of Rafael Camara and join the likes of Piastri and Gabriel Bortoleto as an F3 champion.

title: Sainz on bringing F1 back to his home city of Madrid
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz knows what it's like to have a home Grand Prix, the Spaniard having competed in 12 of them in Formula 1 in Barcelona. He knows how to deliver for his home fans, too, having scored in each of the first 10 of those appearances. But never has he raced in a Formula 1 Grand Prix in his home city of Madrid – until now.

This weekend, he'll compete in the Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid, on a new part-street, part-purpose-built 22-turn circuit called the Madring. The 32-year-old has played a key role in the project from acting as an adviser to helping promote it. The passion he has for the event is infectious.

"I've been lucky enough to have a home race pretty much all through my career thanks to the Grand Prix in Barcelona," says Sainz when we chat all things Madrid in the Williams hospitality unit. "The fact that it's a lot closer to my [family] home, only 15 minutes by car, and all my family and all my friends are from there, it's probably going to feel even more special.

title: 8 of the best debut Grands Prix in F1 history
excerpt:
F1 is heading to Madrid to race at a brand-new track this coming weekend, with the hugely exciting Madring set to make its bow as part of the 2026 season.

The drivers will have to contend with looming walls, some extreme banking and hot temperatures in Spain, meaning the world of F1 could be in for a very exciting weekend.

But while we patiently wait to see the cars hit the Madring later this week, let’s take a look at the sort of racing other tracks threw up in their inaugural Grand Prix.

From Championship fights to crashes, mechanical failures to team mate disputes, a few tracks certainly had debuts to remember…

Las Vegas 2023 – Glitz, glamour and plenty of drama

While Las Vegas had previously hosted the Caesars Palace Grand Prix, the Las Vegas Strip Circuit joined the calendar in 2023 for a spectacular night race against the backdrop of many iconic locations.

Ferrari initially locked out the front row in Qualifying, only for Carlos Sainz to be penalised for needing new PU parts. That left Charles Leclerc on pole and Max Verstappen second, those two delighting fans with wheel-to-wheel racing around the opening lap.

Leclerc emerged in the lead, Verstappen penalised for forcing his rival wide as the City of Lights was treated to some early drama. Sergio Perez also got involved in the battle up front, while Safety Cars meant the front runners diverged on strategy.

George Russell and Verstappen clashed at one point, Lando Norris crashed out and Fernando Alonso spun in a race where grip was at a premium in the cooler night time conditions.

In the end, Verstappen took the win courtesy of a great move on Leclerc, who managed to hold onto second despite Perez briefly also getting past. And as if the racing was not enough, Verstappen then got to pick up his trophy in front of the famous Bellagio fountains to boot.

Miami 2022 – Verstappen wins in the Sunshine State

Miami joined the calendar in 2022, the first year with a new generation of cars. The new track proved a hit too, the picturesque circuit winding its way around the Hard Rock Stadium complex in Miami Gardens.

Red Bull got out of the gates fast in 2022, with Verstappen the favourite to defend his title. The Dutchman won the first race in Miami, but was made to work exceptionally hard for victory with Leclerc hot on his heels for much of the Grand Prix.

Verstappen actually started third, but picked off Sainz and Leclerc to move into the lead and initially seemed like he would be untroubled from there. But then came a Pierre Gasly/Norris crash, which ripped the wheel off the McLaren and caused a Safety Car.

Some of the field came in for fresh tyres, others stayed out, and when the race resumed Verstappen could not get his hard tyres back up to temperature. He was forced to absorb plenty of pressure from Leclerc, with a freshly shod Perez also making moves from behind.

But the Dutchman just about hung on for the win, and did indeed go on to defend his title in 2022.

Saudi Arabia 2021 – Title rivals go head-to-head

When Saudi Arabia’s Jeddah Corniche Circuit arrived on the calendar in 2021, anticipation was high for a track that boasted some incredible speeds, with conditions set to be incredibly testing for the whole field.

The drama in Jeddah started on Saturday, when Verstappen crashed in Qualifying and lost his chance to start on pole. That left rival Lewis Hamilton to take the top spot, and he initially led from pole at the start of the race.

Madring shares new photos ahead of Madrid's maiden GP

But the drama never let up on Sunday, with two pivotal red flag stoppages shaking things up. After the first, Verstappen went wide and cut back onto the track ahead of Hamilton, who also lost out to Esteban Ocon – before two crashes behind halted proceedings once again.

The next restart saw Ocon start ahead of Hamilton with Verstappen third, before the Dutchman took the lead when the others tangled. That was not enough drama though, with three VSC periods shaking things up once again. Before the chequered flag fell, there was also contact between Verstappen and Hamilton, the former told to cede position but doing so in such a place that the latter was caught unawares and he hit the rear wing of the Red Bull.

And for final measure, the two went side by side again, Verstappen running wide to retain the lead and in the end the stewards got involved. It proved a reasonably bad tempered affair, but crucially saw Hamilton draw level on points with his rival…

Portimao 2020 – A new venue in an unusual season

Portugal had hosted F1 races before, but in 2020, Portimao answered the call as the sport managed to return to racing amidst the Covid-19 pandemic. The Algarve International Circuit is set to return again next season, which based on past results bodes very well for the sport.

In 2020, Hamilton was putting together a dominant season for Mercedes. He recorded his 92nd Grand Prix victory at the circuit, to break Michael Schumacher’s long-standing record for most race wins.

That was not the only thing Portimao was remembered for, with differing strategies in play causing plenty of overtakes in the early stages.

Sainz wound up leading from seventh on the grid after the opening exchanges, before Mercedes were able to recover – leading to an intra-team fight between Hamilton and Valtteri Bottas, with the former taking one of the 11 victories he amassed across the season.

Azerbaijan 2016 – Rosberg takes the win on his title charge

The 2016 season will always be remembered for the fight at Mercedes between title holder Hamilton and team mate Nico Rosberg. It was the latter who took the inaugural win in Baku, at what was then named the European Grand Prix.

Rosberg was relatively untroubled around the unique city circuit, which has long wide straights, right-angled corners and then the tight and twisty castle section. But behind there was trouble brewing for his team mate.

Hamilton was struggling with reliability woes, climbing to fourth from a P10 grid slot before falling back with an ERS issue. That loss of points was one of many moments across the season he can point to as to where the title got away.

But while there was little joy for Hamilton, there was plenty for the fans with an action-packed race stuffed full of overtakes, with Baku delivering the goods – something it has continued to do ever since.

Turkey 2005 – Raikkonen makes late bid to stop Alonso’s charge

When Turkey joined the world of F1 in 2005, there was a clash of eras going on, with Fernando Alonso putting together a championship charge as Michael Schumacher’s dominance began to fade. But there was a third driver in play, with Kimi Raikkonen trying to haul a slower-starting McLaren to the title.

Raikkonen started on pole at Istanbul Park, the circuit immediately proving popular with drivers and fans alike. The Finn wound up taking the victory, but it was what was going on behind that added plenty of spice to proceedings.

Juan Pablo Montoya was running second, but collided with a back marker late on which allowed Alonso through to take P2, and some crucial extra championship points. Meanwhile, Schumacher and Mark Webber had a coming together too, in a race filled with incidents.

Despite a late run of victories, neither McLaren driver could overhaul Alonso who went on to take his maiden championship title in 2005.

Malaysia 1999 – A comeback race in attritional conditions

Malaysia joined the calendar in 1999 and was remembered as Schumacher’s comeback race, the German having sustained a broken leg in Silverstone earlier in the season. But it was also notable for how hard it was on drivers and cars, with just 11 finishers seeing the chequered flag.

There was some Ferrari shenanigans in play in Sepang, with a dominant Schumacher dropping behind Eddie Irvine to try and back the pack up, aiding his team mate’s title chances. Somehow Schumacher did manage to keep everyone at bay, with the Scuderia scoring a 1-2.

The drama did not stop when the track action ended though, with both scarlet cars disqualified for a technical breach, only to be reinstated on appeal.

So, all in all, Malaysia certainly delivered a first race to remember.

Hungary 1986 – One of the great overtakes

While Hungary had hosted a race back in the thirties, the Hungaroring joined the calendar in what was a historic first race behind the Iron Curtain in 1986. The track is often compared to a go-kart ring and it is easy to see why, with a series of sweeping corners and very few straights.

But the inaugural Grand Prix will always be remembered for one of the great overtaking moments in F1 history. Nelson Piquet dived around the outside of Ayrton Senna’s Lotus into Turn 1 and he managed to just hold his Williams ahead as he got sideways through the corner – the two just avoiding contact.

Piquet went on to win the race from Senna and team mate Nigel Mansell, who in third finished a lap down in a Grand Prix where 16 cars did not make it to the flag.

title: What is the weather forecast for the Spanish Grand Prix?
excerpt:
The 2026 Formula 1 season continues this weekend with the Spanish Grand Prix, taking place at the newly-built Madring in the nation's capital – but what kind of weather conditions are in store for the drivers and teams?

It currently looks like it'll be another warm and dry event, similar to the previous round held in Italy, with temperatures set to peak at 32C.

In good news for the teams, they won't have to face the challenge of any rain to complicate the circuit's debut, as the likelihood stands at a consistent 0% throughout the weekend.

title: What tyres will the teams have for the Spanish Grand Prix?
excerpt:
The Madring will make its debut on the Formula 1 calendar when it hosts Round 14, the Spanish Grand Prix – and tyre suppliers Pirelli have confirmed the compounds that will be in use throughout the weekend.

Pirelli will provide the drivers and teams with their C2 (as the hard), C3 (as the medium) and C4 (as the soft) compounds at the brand-new track, with tyre management likely to be a big talking point due to the smooth surface.

Drivers will get two sets of the hard tyre (marked white), three sets of the medium tyre (marked yellow), and eight sets of the soft tyre (marked red), as well as access to the green intermediate tyre and the blue full wets, should they be required.

An extra set of softs is reserved for those who reach Q3 in Qualifying, while all drivers must use at least two different slick compounds during the race, providing the track is dry.

"The start-finish line and Turn 1 are separated by just 200 metres," reads Pirelli's weekend preview. "The first sector is very fast and leads into a second section featuring several medium and low-speed corners, including the banked Turn 12. The final part of the lap also includes a number of 90-degree corners similar to those drivers encounter in Baku.

"Pirelli's work to identify the forces that tyres will be subjected to at the Madring began three years ago, when the designers provided the first information on the final layout. Using simulation tools, the trajectories that the cars would follow around the circuit were identified and, consequently, the loads to which the tyres would be exposed were calculated.

"Once the circuit had been completed, a group of Pirelli engineers visited the venue to measure the asphalt's macro and micro roughness, refine the simulations and produce a technical briefing document that was shared with the teams to support their preparation for this new event.

"From an energy perspective, the Madrid circuit ranks among the five most demanding on the calendar, with lateral forces comparable in intensity to those recorded at Barcelona and Silverstone. The "Monumental" is the corner that generates the highest vertical load of the season, not only because of its banking but also because of its length.

"Its configuration will also present a significant challenge in terms of tyre grip. Drivers may adopt different approaches when tackling it, depending on how much they wish to prioritise the opportunity to attack into the following corner.

"The asphalt is very smooth and therefore offers a relatively low level of grip. For this reason, it has been treated with high-pressure water jets, as is already done at other circuits, including Singapore, to remove dust and oily residues typically associated with newly laid surfaces."

title: Kimi Raikkonen's son joins Red Bull Junior Team
excerpt:
Red Bull have announced the signing of Robin Raikkonen, son of 2007 World Champion Kimi Raikkonen, to their driver development programme.

The 11-year-old, who is also known by the nickname 'Ace', will officially start working with the team from 2027 onwards to further his racing career.

Red Bull have proven over the years that they have one of the strongest junior programmes in Formula 1, with their graduates including Max Verstappen, Carlos Sainz and this season's sole rookie Arvid Lindblad.

Identified as "one of the most promising young talents of his generation", the young Raikkonen has already demonstrated his skill in various karting championships and will be supported through the ranks.

Former Ferrari racer Raikkonen said: "We are all thrilled and excited that Robin has been chosen to further his racing path as a member of the Red Bull Junior Team. Laurent [Mekies] and everyone else at Red Bull have been incredibly supportive throughout all our discussions.

"They offer a compelling and comprehensive programme to develop and nurture Robin’s progress over the coming years and provide him with all the experience required to develop his natural talent, which has amply been displayed in all his karting endeavours to date.

"Red Bull’s Junior Team has had years of incredible success. Its alumni include Sebastian Vettel and Verstappen amongst many others. It is thus with great humility that Robin joins this illustrious programme, and he will dedicate all his efforts to warrant the trust that Red Bull is placing in him.”

"Robin has already demonstrated exceptional ability in karting," added Red Bull Team Principal Mekies. "His speed, racecraft and natural talent have established him as one of the most promising young drivers in his age group. At the same time, he impresses with his maturity, his calm approach and his clear focus on driving.

"Our goal is to develop him step by step, without placing any unnecessary pressure on his shoulders. The path through motorsport is a long one, and we will give him the time, support and resources he needs to maximise his potential.

"We strongly believe that talent can thrive when supported by the right people, the right culture and the right environment. That is what we are committed to providing Robin as he continues his development. We are very much looking forward to taking the next steps in his journey together with Robin and his family."

title: Audi point to Red Bull influence behind stunning F1 turnaround
excerpt:
Audi boss Allan McNish has pointed to the influence of former Red Bull chief mechanic Lee Stevenson for the team's turnaround in trackside operations, including pit-stops.

Stevenson, who rose through the Red Bull ranks to become chief mechanic to Max Verstappen, left in 2024 to join Sauber/Stake as it prepared for Audi's 2026 arrival.

Stevenson has now been promoted into the team manager role at Audi, a role similar to that which Jonathan Wheatley held at Red Bull, during which time his pit-crew was regarded as the best in the pit-lane, holding the world record for the fastest pit-stop until McLaren pinched it at the 2023 Qatar GP with a 1.8s stop for Lando Norris.

At the Dutch and Italian Grands Prix, Audi set the fastest pit-stop during the races, a remarkable rise from 2024 when the team was battling a costly technical issue in its stops, involving the wheel nuts.

Reflecting on the efforts at Zandvoort and Monza, racing director McNish pointed to Stevenson's influence on the team's trackside operations.

"It was a technical issue; it was in 2024, actually, and it was the technical issue at that point," McNish told media, including RacingNews365, when first presented with a question about the pit-stops.

"And this has been an area that's been worked on really through the end of last year, beginning of this year. In terms of the team, so Lee, who came to us last year, middle of 2025, he's got a good feel for what we needed to do.

"At the end of the day, the team there is the same people pretty much, and they're delivering it very, very well and consistently now. Because in Zandvoort, it was always the quickest as well, and also the other thing from my point of view, it's not just necessarily one stop, but when we have multiple stops, all the stops are good, and so the team there are working very well.

"That's important for us as well because we've got to take every advantage out of the race that we can. It's not as if there's much of a delta in this midfield, and so they've definitely delivered the opportunity for the drivers to take more out of the race.

"I wouldn't say we inherited [Stevenson's strengths], but I think we we have developed it. But at the end of the day, that was one of the reasons that Lee came on board was to build the team within the garage.

"I think he and the team that's in there have done a very good job. You just see them now, the way that they conduct not just the pit stops but also all of the work on the cars. It's very good to see."

title: Liam Lawson details confidence boost ahead of Madrid F1 debut
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has detailed where he has found extra confidence as he prepares for his third outing this season with Red Bull.

The New Zealander will continue to stand in for Isack Hadjar for the Spanish Grand Prix this weekend, with the latter recovering from a wrist injury.

The Madring in Madrid is hosting F1 for the first time, and the tight, high-speed corners are expected to pose a challenge for the drivers.

Having experienced the new track in the simulator only, Lawson insisted it is impossible to guess where it will stack up in the pecking order until after practice.

“Madrid is going to be an interesting weekend for everyone,” Lawson said.

“We've only run the track in the simulator so far, so the first practice session will tell us a lot about where we really stand.

“It's a unique circuit and the banked corner should make things interesting.”

Lawson endured a difficult weekend last time out at Monza, as a grid penalty for a new engine demoted him to the back of the field.

He was only able to climb as far as 14th - his lowest classification of the year.

However, Lawson insisted he is feeling positive as he pointed to the pace that both he and Red Bull unlocked throughout the event.

“Monza was a challenging weekend from the start with the engine change putting us on the back foot, so it was difficult to fully show what we were capable of,” he said.

“The positive is that we found some good pace as the weekend progressed, which gives us confidence heading into Madrid."

title: Oscar Piastri explains 'quite bizarre' Italian GP battle with Lewis Hamilton
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri has explained that it is "still quite bizarre" how energy management works as part of the new regulations this season, following a battle with Lewis Hamilton at Monza.

Piastri enjoyed one of his strongest weekends of the season at the Italian Grand Prix, finishing in fifth but, for large portions of the race, looking in with a shot at a possible podium.

Unfortunately for the Australian, his rostrum chances were ruined by a back-and-forth battle with Hamilton.

The pair squabbled over fourth before Piastri broke away; however, the seven-time world champion suddenly caught the McLaren driver and overtook him by using a significant amount of battery.

Once ahead, Hamilton continued to use what was left in his battery to get almost one second ahead before it depleted, and he was almost immediately re-overtaken by Piastri.

Energy management was a critical factor in Monza and remains something very unusual for the drivers to experience, as Piastri explained after fighting the Ferrari.

Asked if playing a thinking game with energy management was fun, Piastri told select media, including RacingNews365: "It's difficult. Like, if you use any extra energy, you're going to pay for it somewhere.

"And I was kind of slowly building a gap on Lewis, and then he spent all his energy getting past me, and then kind of kept using it to try and break free. And he actually got, like, a second ahead, and he lost it all in one straight. So it's still quite bizarre.

"Did I enjoy it more than I thought? Yes. Was I stuck in a lot of battles that I just wanted to go and have them pull me further into the race? Yes. I was also in that situation, so it is what it is.

"Probably better than a race where nothing happens, but definitely difficult in the cockpit to know exactly what to do."

title: The Senna-fication of Kimi Antonelli
excerpt:
In F1, every generation, a driver comes along with talent or dedication to their craft so supreme that they move the needle for what was thought possible, for how good or how dominant anyone dared believe someone could be.

Juan Manuel Fangio conquered the 1950s, before Jim Clark assumed the mantle in the 60s. Then Jackie Stewart bridged to Niki Lauda in the 70s.

The 1980s had two, in Alain Prost and Ayrton Senna, and then Michael Schumacher turned up at Spa-Francorchamps in 1991, and, over the next 15 years, he pushed the boundaries of what was known to be achievable in Formula 1.

He retired ­— for the first time — at the end of 2006, and the seven-time F1 drivers’ champion was immediately replaced by a driver who would become another, Lewis Hamilton.

A decade or so later, Max Verstappen, aged just 17, took Formula 1 by storm. A teenage phenom who would win his first grand prix before most people have even left school.

And now, there’s Kimi Antonelli, and he looks set to comfortably take the crown for the youngest driver to win the crown.

If and when he does, the young Italian will smash Sebastian Vettel’s record by three years, having been a teenager himself for most of the campaign.

The Italian is taking the baton from Verstappen, who carried on from Hamilton and Schumacher before him.

What started with Fangio has adapted and evolved, reshaped itself to fit and suit the times. Arguments for a greatest of all time are reductive and imperfect, but there is almost always a defining driver of a generation, emblematic of an era, adorned in nostalgia and folklore.

And that, precisely, is where Senna stands alone — for now. Maybe it’s because he lost his life in pursuit of the elusive greatest that graces so few.

He is not the only great Formula 1 driver to die in a racing car, but he is often placed on a pedestal.

If you asked 100 people who they thought was the best F1 driver of all time, I’d put money on the largest share of the votes going to the Brazilian; he holds a unique stature in the sport.

The signs were there before the Italian Grand Prix, but Antonelli's exploits at Monza, on home turf, give the impression that what he may have been tentatively etching in pencil will one day be made permanent in pen.

Like an AI agent

Full disclosure, I’ve always been more of a Prost person, which is why I’ve maybe found the deification of Senna peculiar, and perhaps slightly over the top.

Maybe it’s because I never lived to see the three-time F1 drivers’ champion race, the majesty of his talent, the breathtaking nature of his abilities that replays can only partially do justice to — I was born just months before that fateful weekend at Imola in 1994.

There is no doubting his brilliance, but to my earlier point, had it been Prost in that Williams that day, maybe things would be viewed differently. And maybe I would feel differently.

But now, I’m left with the unshakable feeling that Antonelli is slowly starting to write his name alongside Senna’s.

The signs were there before the Italian Grand Prix, but Antonelli's exploits at Monza, on home turf, give the impression that what he may have been tentatively etching in pencil will one day be made permanent in pen.

It is no surprise to see the eulogisation of his performance at the Temple of Speed, for Monza is hallowed ground. For Antonelli to do what he did where he did it, at the altar of the Tifosi, where Ferrari is religion, is something quite incredible.

And what makes it all the more remarkable is how unremarkable it all seemed; it was that remarkable.

It was so astonishing that it looked almost ordinary, like it really was no bother to him at all, like he is capable of accessing a higher plane that mere mortals and most others on the grid can only dream of — and all at the age of just 20.

P19 to first. Unreal. Sure, the red flag fell in his favour, and so did strategy (eventually), but it was a masterclass. When all is said and done, it could stand to be his magnum opus. At the least, it feels seminal.

So, it was scarcely unexpected when Toto Wolff said afterwards that he had a feeling Antonelli would "walk over water", a direct reference to Jesus, and later, when he compared the seven-time grand prix winner to an "AI agent" that "continuously self-improves and learns" because of the speed at which he is developing.

And he did make George Russell — who performed well in the other Mercedes — look human.

Antonelli's seminal moment

Senna famously had one of those formative successes — in Monaco during his debut F1 season in 1984, when he, in torrential conditions, dragged his Toleman to second. And it would have been victory, had Prost not been able to, in part, convince the officials to call the race off on safety grounds.

That was when, to many, it first became clear that Senna was special, that he would be special.

And Monza was the perfect place for Antonelli to have his moment. You could argue Imola would have been more fitting, given it’s his home circuit, and because it’s where Senna lost his life, but Imola is no longer on the F1 calendar, even though it may well host the season finale, where Antonelli is looking increasingly likely to end his first title-winning campaign.

But the Temple of Speed is home to potentially the lowest point of Antonelli’s journey to here, when two years ago, he crashed at the Curva Alboreto (or the Parabolica), just 10 minutes into what was shaping up to be a mighty impressive FP1 debut.

Coincidentally, Michele Alboreto is the last Italian to fight for the F1 drivers’ championship, in 1985. Giancarlo Fisichella led the hunt for a round, two decades later, but only because he won the season-opening Australian Grand Prix.

And last year at Monza, Wolff called out Antonelli’s poor performance as "underwhelming". 12 months on, he recounted telling him he needed to "wake up" after a torrid European leg of the schedule.

That all plays into the significance of Monza, where pivotal moments seem in rich supply for Antonelli.

Watching him stand on the podium after his triumph, in front of the sea of red, you could sense passionate Ferrari fans, who have long held Italian drivers at arm’s length with an icy regard, continue to warm to him, as they have done so across the current campaign; how that winter of discontent is beginning to thaw.

Antonelli is becoming embraced, the first Italian to win at Monza in 60 years. Unlike those who came before him, he is approaching uncharted territory.

Driver

Ayrton Senna

Brazilian

Unique legacy

Senna is adored, understandably so, and Antonelli is well on his way.

But he is the first to highlight his dislike of comparisons. That’s fair enough; he is so early in his career, and Mercedes has sought to shield him from the accompanying pressure and the weight of expectation.

Don’t get me wrong, there are no guarantees in F1, or in life more generally. Antonelli’s potential and initial signs of promise have the markings of an extraordinary career, but that doesn’t mean it will play out that way.

But Senna has his own unique legacy. And Antonelli can have his.

Like Verstappen, Hamilton and Schumacher, Senna was divisive. Polarising figures, of which Antonelli is not — at least not yet.

So, it’s not the hair and the resemblance, or the fact that the Brazilian is his idol — or that he chose to race under the number 12 that became synonymous with his hero — that are the true foundations of this particular comparison; it’s that Antonelli, too, has the opportunity to leave his own indelible mark.

And he can achieve that by doing it differently, by moving the needle again and separating himself.

© XPBimages

Walk over water?

Asked whether Antonelli’s performance at Monza was definitive evidence that his driver is the complete package, and that what was just achieved was the final piece of the jigsaw, Wolff cut to the very heart of what the Italian has a chance to do.

"When you talk about the complete driver, the aspect of experience is still missing; that needs to come," he said.

"There is also that he has this easiness of a young man that helps to overcome difficult moments. That also helps in managing not getting ahead of himself when having these glorious moments.

"There is the fact of whether he is capable of maturing, of staying the personality that he is — humble, with a lot of introspection, self-criticism — in order to develop, and that only the future is going to show whether he is, like a few drivers before him, the complete deal."

If Lando Norris proved last year that you can win championships as the antithesis of the overtly flawed and stereotypical athlete, perhaps it is Antonelli who will prove you can emulate greatness in the same mould, by being dominant but not divisive.

We don’t know how much he will go on to win, or how much he might achieve, or even how he will go about doing it, if he does at all. But on Sunday at Monza, you got the sense that Antonelli is starting to tread that path.

Walk over walk? Perhaps not. Walk in the footsteps of Senna and unique legacy? Maybe.

title: What is behind Fernando Alonso's F1 contract delay?
excerpt:
Madrid hosts F1’s Spanish Grand Prix this weekend, however, it appears that the wait for updates regarding two-time world champion Fernando Alonso’s future will continue.

9 September 5:30PM

Although the upcoming Spanish Grand Prix at the brand-new Madring looks to be an ideal opportunity to confirm Fernando Alonso's future in F1, RacingNews365’s sources indicate that the wait is set to be prolonged, and no announcement is expected this weekend.

Alonso's contract with Aston Martin expires at the end of the season, and the future of the F1 grid's two-time world champion veteran has been a major talking point since the start of the season.

Since the Silverstone-based team, which began using Honda powertrains this year, started the 2026 season with a performance well below expectations, numerous rumours regarding the driver's intentions and options have arisen in recent months.

One possible scenario was a return for a fourth chapter to the site of his greatest successes, Enstone, to Alpine, where his manager, Flavio Briatore, is once again at the helm.

However, with Pierre Gasly under contract until the end of 2028 and the team having recently extended Franco Colapinto’s deal for 2027, this door has closed.

The 45-year-old driver has previously denied speculations about his retirement on numerous occasions, leaving the option of staying at Aston Martin and continuing to race for the green team in 2027, and perhaps beyond.

As the number of possible scenarios has dwindled and there are no reasonable alternatives left on the driver market, it is logical that the parties are in no rush to make an announcement, especially considering that there is still a lot of work to be done within the struggling team.

The talks between the driver and team are also thought to be complex. It is a safe bet that following this year's extreme struggles, team owner Lawrence Stroll will compensate Alonso, who is treated as the crown jewel, with a pay raise.

But the duration of the extension is likely also a major topic in the negotiations. Some sources suggest a one-plus-one-year new contract is probable, while they are presumably also discussing what title or position the Spaniard could receive within the Aston Martin universe after retiring from his racing career.

Trust and loyalty in the middle of the struggles

In recent weeks, Alonso has openly declared multiple times that he plans to continue with Aston Martin, and these circles are saying that he is eagerly looking forward to finally racing in a car entirely designed by Adrian Newey.

In Monza, the Spaniard once again emphasised that he is confident Honda can resolve its agonising problems.

“100%,” Alonso replied when asked whether he thinks the Japanese manufacturer can be as successful as it was recently as Red Bull's partner.

“I think it's a huge commitment from Honda.

“The facilities we have in Japan are one of the best. I think the personnel and the management of the power unit now has been reinforced on the set. A lot of people that were in the previous project, they are in again on this one.

“I think I have no doubts. I 100% trust Honda. We just need to shortcut somehow that process. Unfortunately we started with the wrong foot.

“We started with this set of regulations not at the level that we wanted. But I have no doubts that they will get there.

“As I said many times, we don't want to wait five years like they did last time. We want to do it in two or three years maximum.”

Aston Martin is keen to keep hold of Alonso going forward, with the team's trackside officer Mike Krack outlining that it is respecting the Spaniard's approach.

“The whole situation is clear. We know where we want to go,” he said.

“We wait, we respect Fernando requesting time to think and making sure that he's in a good place.

“With a driver with this much experience and this record, it's a matter of respect just to acknowledge that and to wait.

“As I said before, I'm quite confident that we can find a good solution, and then we are strong for the future.”

title: Max Verstappen outlines greatest desire for post-F1 career
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has set his sights on taking part in endurance racing once he opts to bring his F1 career to an end.

The four-time champion has long voiced his appreciation for endurance competition and often takes part in virtual events on his simulator.

He also dipped his toes into the world earlier this year with an appearance at the 24 Hours of Nurburgring, having had several outings at the Nordschleife in preparation for the event.

Verstappen recently extended his Red Bull contract until the end of 2030 as he targets a return to the front of the field with the Milton Keynes-based squad.

But having already had a taste of endurance racing, Verstappen insisted that he is only getting started.

When asked what else is on his bucket list, Verstappen told BBC Sport: "All the endurance races.

“Eventually, of course also Hypercar [the world endurance championship]. I don't want to rush it.

“I want to do it in the right environment. On my terms. And competitive."

In the past, it has been suggested that Verstappen and Fernando Alonso could team up for an entry at the 24 Hours of Le Mans - the most prestigious endurance race.

Verstappen has confirmed he has discussed the possibility with his fellow champion, but admitted scheduling conflicts could get in the way.

"We've talked about it. I mean, look at Fernando,” Verstappen said.

“He's 45 and he's still flying. Especially for Le Mans, with his experience, it could be a good option. It needs to fit our schedules.

“It needs to make sense. It needs to be on my terms. And there needs to be a real chance to go there and win it."

title: F1 driver remains conscious after 'violent' airborne crash - On This Day
excerpt:
On this day 36 years ago, former F1 driver Derek Warwick suffered a terrifying accident in Monza yet managed to restart the race!

On 9 September 1990, Ayrton Senna delivered a masterclass at Monza with a grand slam victory in the Italian Grand Prix. But it was Derek Warwick's extraordinary accident at the Parabolica that remains seared into the memory of everyone who witnessed it.

Warwick, driving the Lotus 102 for Camel Team Lotus, was following Mauricio Gugelmin's car closely at the end of the opening lap when he got caught in the aerodynamic turbulence.

At speeds estimated around 150 mph, the Lotus understeered wide, clipped the grass on the exit of the Parabolica, and struck the barrier with tremendous force.

The impact launched the car into a barrel roll, sending it sliding upside down across the track as debris scattered in all directions. Marshals had to dive clear.

A brief fire broke out before extinguishing itself as the destroyed Lotus came to rest, its survival cell mercifully intact.

Warwick, remarkably, was conscious throughout. He later explained his composure in chillingly matter-of-fact terms: "I was conscious all the time... My first reaction after that was 'I'm okay' and my second was, 'spare car.'"

He climbed out unaided, ran back to the pits, and, after medical checks declared him fit, jumped into the spare Lotus for the restart. His race ultimately ended with a clutch failure, but his survival was the real story.

Senna victory overshadowed

The severity of Warwick's crash triggered an immediate red flag at the end of lap one, with the race restarted over its full 53-lap distance. From there, Senna controlled proceedings from pole to chequered flag, also setting the fastest lap to complete a grand slam for McLaren-Honda.

Alain Prost brought his Ferrari home second, 6.054 seconds adrift, with Gerhard Berger completing the podium in the second McLaren.

Nigel Mansell finished fourth in the other Ferrari, while both Benetton drivers lost time through troublesome pit stops, with the leading cars all running non-stop strategies.

It was Senna's 26th career victory, but the image that endured from that afternoon at Monza was not one of triumph. It was a Lotus sliding on its back through the Parabolica, a driver walking away from wreckage that looked entirely unsurvivable, and then asking for the spare car.

"It was a violent impact but I'm OK, no problem!" Warwick told reporters with characteristic nonchalance. Thirty-six years on, it remains one of the most spectacular survivable accidents the sport has ever seen.

title: 2026 F1 Spanish Grand Prix - Madrid weather forecast
excerpt:
F1 heads to Madrid this weekend for the inaugural Spanish Grand Prix at the brand-new Circuito de Madring, a 5.416km, 22-corner hybrid layout winding around the IFEMA exhibition centre and through the Valdebebas district.

The circuit blends tight, street-style corners in its southern section with faster, flowing sequences to the north, headlined by the spectacular 24%-banked "La Monumental" corner.

It replaces the Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya, which hosted the race since 1991.

As for the conditions greeting drivers on this historic weekend, the paddock should brace itself.

There is no rain expected across any of the three days, but the heat will be relentless.

Friday's opening practice sessions are forecast to see temperatures climb to around 30°C, with a very light southerly breeze offering little in the way of relief.

That warmth will only intensify as the weekend progresses, with Saturday's forecast predicting 31°C during the late afternoon, precisely when qualifying is scheduled.

Managing tyre warm-up could prove tricky in those conditions, as the extreme track surface temperatures may push rubber beyond its optimal operating window before drivers can extract a clean lap.

Sunday, however, looks set to be the most punishing day of all, with 33°C forecast for race day. At that level, it is very likely the FIA will formally declare a Heat Hazard.

Under the current Sporting Regulations, the Race Director initiates the protocol when the official weather forecast predicts a heat index greater than 31.0°C at any point during the grand prix.

Once declared, teams are required to install driver cooling systems in the car, with health monitoring procedures also activated throughout the event.

title: Mercedes boss mindset explored after 'so difficult' team orders decision
excerpt:
Former Formula 1 driver David Coulthard has explored the mindset of Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff, who made the "so difficult" decision to let his drivers race in Monza.

Kimi Antonelli recovered from 19th on the grid to lead home another Mercedes one-two in the Italian Grand Prix, with the youngster taking the lead with three laps remaining.

Not for the first time this season, Antonelli and Russell battled hard across large portions of the race, with the championship leader at one stage going off the circuit.

A call did come to both drivers mid-race to hold position in an attempt to break away from Max Verstappen, which did lead to a brief moment of calm on circuit.

However, that went out of the window in the final laps, when the pair went to battle again for the Monza win. It was a situation where Wolff could have easily instructed the duo not to fight, yet no call came from the Austrian.

Coulthard praised the decision and the pure racer in the Mercedes boss, although he conceded that it must have been an extremely challenging choice to make.

Discussing Wolff not introducing team orders, Coulthard said on the Up to Speed podcast: "It was interesting, but to try and understand how close he was to sort of pushing the radio button to say, 'Right, guys, you know, we just need good points here. Of course, we want to win, but we don't need you tripping over each other.'

"And there was a moment early in the race where they did sort of calm them down. But in the latter stages, when the race came back on, I was going to say, 'I'm proud of Toto,' but who the hell am I to be proud of him?

"But it must be so difficult to not push that button because if you put yourself there, you're a shareholder and the team principal, and you're going to have a one-two.

"Putting your commercial head on, it would be really difficult. Putting your racer's head on, you'd be like, 'Right, bring it. Let's create something for the ages.'"

title: Max Verstappen predicts 'big shunts' at Madrid F1 weekend
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has predicted that there will be some “big shunts” throughout the upcoming Spanish Grand Prix weekend.

The Circuito de Madring will host its first F1 race event in the coming days, becoming the newest track to join the schedule.

The street circuit will pose a high-speed challenge for the drivers as they bid to become the first to stand on the top step of the podium at the venue.

At a recent Formula 3 test from Madrid, 19 red flags were deployed across two days, 11 of which were for contact with the barriers.

It has created speculation that the track could be the scene of multiple collisions throughout the weekend.

When asked if he has driven the track on his home setup, Verstappen replied: “Yeah I did, we also have it on the F1 sim.

“It's going to be very difficult. It's not an easy track. If you do a few laps in a row, it's always hard to cross the line and say 'I nailed the lap'.

“It's very hard. It also has a tendency of creating some big shunts in some places.”

F1 has seen an increase in visits to street circuits in recent years, with Jeddah, Miami and Las Vegas among those that have been included in the calendar.

Verstappen has likened the Madrid track to Jeddah, which is known as one of the most challenging circuits on the schedule.

“It reminds me a little bit of Jeddah in a way, with fast corners and the walls being very close,” he added.

title: Is Lewis Hamilton's eighth F1 title dream dead this year?
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton's Italian Grand Prix was supposed to be a springboard. Instead, it turned into a weekend that may well have ended his championship challenge.

A lap-one clash with teammate Charles Leclerc at the first chicane sent Hamilton tumbling from fourth on the grid to the lower reaches of the midfield, and from there, the damage was done.

Leclerc squeezed him wide, forcing the seven-time world champion off track and into the gravel. One lap later, Leclerc himself was out of the race after a high-speed crash at the Parabolica, leaving Hamilton as Ferrari's sole representative but already buried in the pack.

A questionable strategy call, in which Ferrari opted not to pit Hamilton under a mid-race Virtual Safety Car, compounded the misery.

He was left exposed on the straights, unable to match the straight-line speed of those around him, and eventually crossed the line in sixth, some 24 seconds behind race winner Kimi Antonelli.

"A bit devastating," Hamilton said afterwards. "Tough one to swallow. Lost a lot of points and ultimately couldn't keep a Mercedes engine behind. They were just out and out quicker."

The deficit to championship leader Antonelli now stands at 76 points with likely nine races remaining. Mathematically, it is still possible, but Hamilton himself appeared resigned to the reality of the situation.

"It's never over until it's over," he conceded. "I don't know how many points it is now, but I'm sure it's 60, 70... with the pace that they have, it's a very, very difficult amount to close out."

title: Red Bull announce Kimi Raikkonen's son as latest junior signing
excerpt:
Red Bull has confirmed the signing of Robin Raikkonen, son of F1 champion Kimi, to its F1 junior programme.

RacingNews365 first revealed Raikkonen's signing to Red Bull last weekend during the Italian Grand Prix.

Raikkonen is still in the early stages of his racing career, competing in karting championships as he prepares for a step up to single-seater competition in the coming years.

He now looks set to do so with Red Bull, who has added the Finn to its famous junior squad.

"Robin has already demonstrated exceptional ability in karting,” Red Bull team boss Laurent Mekies said.

“His speed, racecraft and natural talent have established him as one of the most promising young drivers in his age group.

“At the same time, he impresses with his maturity, his calm approach and his clear focus on driving.

“Our goal is to develop him step by step, without placing any unnecessary pressure on his shoulders.

“The path through motorsport is a long one, and we will give him the time, support and resources he needs to maximise his potential.

“We strongly believe that talent can thrive when supported by the right people, the right culture and the right environment. That is what we are committed to providing Robin as he continues his development.

“We are very much looking forward to taking the next steps in his journey together with Robin and his family."

Red Bull has worked with many young drivers throughout its history in motorsport, with its biggest success stories from the programme being Sebastian Vettel and Max Verstappen.

title: Carlos Sainz addresses Madrid F1 concern after red flag chaos
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz has played down the disruption F1 sessions could endure at Madrid next weekend.

The Madring will make its F1 debut when it hosts round 14 of the 2026 season, taking over as the location of the Spanish Grand Prix.

The track has been under construction for several years and recently held an in-season Formula 3 test in anticipation of the maiden race event.

During the test, 19 red flags were deployed across two days, 11 of which were for contact with the barrier.

It has generated concern that it could mean chaos for F1 this weekend, with Sainz acknowledging that the track will be a major challenge.

“With the way they've put the barriers and the design of the track, it's going to be one of the biggest challenges in F1 recently,” he said.

“The track reminds me a lot of Jeddah, reminds me a lot of Baku, even reminds me a bit of Macau in some ways.

“So having that in F1 with 1,000 horsepower is going to be quite an interesting challenge.”

However, Sainz insisted that F1 is no stranger to dealing with the challenge of high-speed street tracks with close barriers.

As a result, he does not expect the weekend to to feature many chaotic incidents.

“Looking at the track and hearing of what happened in the F3 test, I think we are all expecting safety cars and red flags and yellow flags in quali.

“But it's been a fashion or a tendency of F1 to go to these kind of tracks like Jeddah or Baku that are closer to the city.

“They have more walls, and we haven't had any issues with it. The races actually seem to be going quite well at every place we've gone.

“It's that same similar trend that we're going towards.”
